fields.topic_name: Forecast scores vs. trade decisions
fields.description:
Core lesson

A predicted probability or forward return is an estimate of an outcome, not an instruction to buy or sell. A decision policy must specify the opportunity set, decision time, permitted instruments, trade side, expected execution price, and when positions close. Classification probability can be converted to expected move only if conditional move magnitudes are modeled or estimated. Compare a simple score threshold rule against a cost-aware rule. Include a flat state when the forecast is too weak to overcome estimated costs; abstaining is a valid decision.

Worked market example

A model predicts an upward move with probability 0.57, but if the expected upside is 0.4 bps while the round-trip cost is 1.2 bps, a buy decision can still have negative expectancy.

What to read

  • Scikit-learn — tune the decision threshold
  • Scikit-learn — classification and probability metrics
  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Write a precise policy: observation, forecast, entry trigger, exit horizon, and no-trade condition.
  2. Plot forecast scores against realized forward returns in validation data.
  3. Compute approximate expected value after fees and spread for three example forecasts.

Common mistakes and interpretation

A forecast at the mid-price does not imply a trade can enter or exit at mid. Avoid using unseen price moves to determine entry.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Deliver a policy specification separating predicted market outcome from executable trading action.

fields.topic_name: Threshold selection and position sizing
fields.description:
Core lesson

Thresholds determine the tradeoff between signal strength, opportunity count, and execution cost. For a probability model, a 0.5 cutoff is not automatically optimal; set entry thresholds based on validation-only expected outcomes after cost assumptions. Position sizing determines exposure per forecast. Start with fixed notional or fixed unit positions before experimenting with probability-scaled size, which requires calibrated probabilities and risk controls. Define limits such as maximum position, inventory, loss stop, and no-trade spread threshold; justify each using a simple constrained policy.

Worked market example

If a round trip costs 2 bps, a strategy entering whenever predicted move exceeds 0.1 bp is structurally unconvincing. A higher threshold reduces trades but may improve expected net outcome.

What to read

  • Scikit-learn — tune the decision threshold
  • Scikit-learn — probability calibration and reliability diagrams
  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Sweep several threshold levels using validation predictions, recording trade count and gross average return.
  2. Subtract transparent cost estimates and plot net result versus threshold.
  3. Implement capped fixed-size and score-weighted position sizes, then compare concentration.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Do not choose a threshold using the final test. Avoid leverage optimization before you have reliable out-of-sample predictive evidence.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Save a selected threshold with its validation rationale, maximum exposure, and no-trade rules.

fields.topic_name: Turnover, holding periods and risk constraints
fields.description:
Core lesson

Turnover measures trading activity relative to portfolio size, and holding period controls how often spreads and fees are paid. Even an accurate short-horizon signal can lose money if every small price move triggers a trade. Risk constraints include gross and net inventory, max single-instrument exposure, time-in-position, participation limits, and session stop rules. Determine whether consecutive model scores represent independent opportunities or repeated signals while an existing position remains open. Implement policies as explicit state transitions rather than backfilling trade decisions into a PnL column.

Worked market example

If a strategy buys then sells every ten seconds, it may capture 0.3 bps on average in mid-price movement but incur a one-tick spread each round trip, overwhelming the apparent edge.

What to read

  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python
  • QuantStats — performance metrics and reports
  • Scikit-learn — tune the decision threshold

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Compute turnover and average holding period for a simple sequence of long/flat/short states.
  2. Implement maximum position and minimum holding-time constraints.
  3. Plot inventory, trade count, and exposure by session under three policy variants.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Overlapping positions and repeated forecasts can cause double-counting. Define whether reversals close an existing position before opening the opposite side.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Produce an executable state machine with tests for inventory caps and deterministic transitions.

fields.topic_name: Translate model forecasts into hypothetical long/short/flat signals
fields.description:
Core lesson

Converting forecasts to long/short/flat states requires a deterministic policy that reads predictions at their actual availability time. A symmetric rule might buy above an upper probability threshold, short below a lower threshold, and otherwise remain flat, but asymmetric spreads or shorting restrictions may justify different cutoffs. Specify whether the decision is a target position or an immediate order; the latter introduces fill uncertainty. Preserve a chronological event log of every decision and its inputs so backtesting can replay it without consulting future labels.

Worked market example

At t=100 a score of 0.64 may request long one unit. If the next score is 0.53 and the flat zone begins below 0.55, the policy requests exit—not necessarily a filled sale.

What to read

  • Scikit-learn — tune the decision threshold
  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python
  • Scikit-learn — pipelines and composite estimators

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Implement a pure function from current position and score to target long/short/flat state.
  2. Generate a decision ledger with timestamp, score, threshold, and prior position.
  3. Write unit tests for threshold equality, missing predictions, market close, and position limit behavior.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Never populate decisions by iterating over future return columns. Model decisions and executions as separate records.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Deliver an auditable signal ledger and state-transition tests ready to connect to a simulator.

fields.topic_name: Choose thresholds using training/validation data only
fields.description:
Core lesson

Threshold selection is part of model development and must be frozen before an untouched evaluation. Use walk-forward validation predictions to compare a small prespecified grid of cutoffs; calculate trades, gross edge, estimated costs, and net edge for each. Prefer a broad stable plateau over one narrow peak. Check sensitivity to doubled costs, wider spreads, and different sessions. Save the selected thresholds with a versioned policy definition and never recalibrate them based on the final test's realized PnL.

Worked market example

A 0.62 entry threshold might appear best at 0.7 bps per trade, but thresholds 0.60–0.64 may be statistically indistinguishable. Choose a robust range rather than the most flattering point.

What to read

  • Scikit-learn — tune the decision threshold
  • Statsmodels — multiple-test correction
  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Evaluate a limited threshold grid on validation-only records using identical execution assumptions.
  2. Plot estimated net bps/trade and number of trades against threshold.
  3. Freeze the chosen policy, record its creation date, and generate a final-test command without retuning.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Selecting the best of hundreds of thresholds is multiple testing; count the search and report the selection process.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Finish Week 9 with a versioned score-to-position policy and a validation-only decision report.

fields.topic_name: Spread, fees, slippage, funding and adverse selection
fields.description:
Core lesson

Backtesting at the mid-price is often an optimistic accounting exercise. An aggressive buy normally executes against the ask, and an aggressive sell against the bid, introducing spread cost before commissions and fees. Slippage includes variation between intended and actual prices; market impact is your own order's effect on price. Adverse selection occurs when the trades that fill are disproportionately those followed by unfavorable price moves. Futures, equities, and FX have different fee models and funding assumptions; express each in consistent price, ticks, or basis-point units.

Worked market example

If bid/ask is 100.00/100.02, a one-share market buy and immediate market sell loses 0.02 before fees, even though the mid-price has not moved.

What to read

  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python
  • LOBSTER — event and order-book field definitions
  • Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov — The Price Impact of Order Book Events

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Calculate transaction PnL for market buy/sell round trips at several spreads.
  2. Implement configurable commissions and an additional slippage assumption per fill.
  3. Compute gross and net returns for a toy signal and identify the break-even expected move.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Do not treat a midpoint crossing as a guaranteed fill. Validate that the market convention and currency units match the instrument.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Produce a cost function with unit tests for long, short, and round-trip examples.

fields.topic_name: Latency, fills, queue position and market impact
fields.description:
Core lesson

A realistic fill model needs decision timestamp, submission delay, venue arrival time, order type, and available liquidity. A market order may cross a spread and walk depth; a limit order enters a queue, and a later touch of its price does not prove a fill. Queue position often cannot be reconstructed accurately from aggregated L2 snapshots; mark the simulation as a conservative approximation. Adverse selection can make passive fills look cheap while subsequent prices move against you. Test how outcomes change when execution latency increases and fill probability decreases.

Worked market example

An order posted at the best bid is not filled simply because a later trade prints at that bid. Older orders ahead in the queue may have priority.

What to read

  • LOBSTER — event and order-book field definitions
  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python
  • Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov — The Price Impact of Order Book Events

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Sketch the timeline from model observation to order arrival and fill/cancel.
  2. Implement aggressive fills at the next eligible displayed quote, with configurable latency.
  3. Compare optimistic passive, conservative passive, and aggressive execution assumptions on toy events.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Avoid claiming exchange-level fill realism from L2 data. Do not execute using a quote that precedes the modeled order-arrival time.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Deliver fill-model assumptions in plain language and tests demonstrating outcomes under added latency.

fields.topic_name: Sharpe, drawdown, turnover and capacity
fields.description:
Core lesson

Sharpe ratio measures average excess return per unit of return volatility under chosen sampling assumptions; blindly annualizing irregular intraday strategy returns can be misleading. Maximum drawdown measures the largest peak-to-trough equity decline. Turnover counts how aggressively exposure changes, and capacity asks whether the strategy still works at greater size when liquidity and impact matter. Report trade count, mean net bps, hit rate, exposure time, drawdown, and cost sensitivity, not a lone Sharpe number. Distinguish profit per trade from portfolio returns with a defined capital base.

Worked market example

A strategy with a high gross win rate and very few trades may produce a fragile Sharpe estimate; one large losing fill can dominate realized drawdown.

What to read

  • QuantStats — performance metrics and reports
  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python
  • Statsmodels — statistical inference and tests

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Calculate cumulative net PnL and maximum drawdown on a synthetic series.
  2. Compute turnover, trading frequency, and per-trade net bps from execution records.
  3. Write a dashboard with Sharpe assumptions, session PnL, and trade counts clearly labeled.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Do not annualize per-trade returns as if they were daily independent portfolio returns; explain the sampling frequency and capital denominator.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Provide a metric definition sheet and a backtest performance report with drawdown and cost sensitivity.

fields.topic_name: Develop a conservative event-driven simulator
fields.description:
Core lesson

An event-driven simulator processes ordered events rather than applying vectorized future returns to a signal column. Design a minimal engine with market-data events, model-signal events, order requests, fills, and portfolio updates. At each timestamp, record what the policy knows, update outstanding orders, simulate eligible execution using later market states, and then mark inventory to market. Keep decision time, arrival time, and fill time separate. For a 60-minute build, prioritize correct event order and tests over a full exchange matching engine.

Worked market example

A signal created at 10:00:00.100 with 50 ms latency cannot fill using the 10:00:00.110 quote. The first eligible market data comes after 10:00:00.150.

What to read

  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python
  • LOBSTER — event and order-book field definitions
  • QuantStats — performance metrics and reports

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Define simple dataclasses for Quote, Signal, Order, Fill, and PortfolioState.
  2. Implement chronological event processing and marketable-order execution with fixed latency.
  3. Write tests that prohibit fills before arrival and verify cash/inventory reconciliation.

Common mistakes and interpretation

This is not a complete exchange simulator: queue position, hidden liquidity, partial fills, and cross-venue routing may remain approximated.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Finish with a reproducible toy replay and a fill ledger proving the event-order constraints.

fields.topic_name: Report net results under pessimistic cost assumptions
fields.description:
Core lesson

A convincing quantitative research report shows what remains after conservative trading assumptions. Evaluate a frozen signal under base, adverse, and severe scenarios: tighter versus wider spreads, higher fees, additional latency, lower fill rates, and reduced participation. Distinguish realized sample PnL from claims about future performance. Present the distribution of daily net outcomes, not just cumulative equity. If simulated profitability disappears under plausible costs, write that plainly and analyze whether the project still demonstrates valuable predictive or engineering insights.

Worked market example

A gross average of +1.4 bps/trade becomes -0.3 bps after 1.7 bps costs. Doubling spread cost to 2.8 bps makes the weakness clearer, regardless of the predictive accuracy.

What to read

  • QuantStart — event-driven backtesting in Python
  • QuantStats — performance metrics and reports
  • Statsmodels — multiple-test correction

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Run your frozen signal through three explicit cost and latency scenarios.
  2. Calculate net bps/trade, turnover, and drawdown for each scenario.
  3. Write a conclusion separating forecasting success from economically executable strategy success.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Do not quietly optimize the signal again after observing the harsh scenario results; that requires a new experiment with a new evaluation period.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Deliver Week 10’s backtest report with a scenario table, execution assumptions, and independent reproducibility steps.

fields.topic_name: Financial text embeddings and retrieval
fields.description:
Core lesson

A text embedding converts a sentence or document into a fixed-length numeric vector intended to capture semantic similarity. Sentence Transformers can encode financial headlines, filing excerpts, and short event descriptions, but general-purpose embeddings are not trained specifically to predict returns. Retrieval ranks documents by similarity to a query; it is useful for exploring disclosures or identifying related events, not evidence of market forecasting power. Define the text unit, tokenizer/truncation behavior, and embedding model version. Document usage rights and avoid storing confidential news content in a public repository.

Worked market example

The phrases “guidance raised” and “earnings outlook improved” may yield similar embeddings, while “guidance cut” should ideally rank differently; semantic similarity alone does not encode a correct trading direction.

What to read

  • Sentence Transformers — quickstart and embeddings
  • Sentence Transformers — semantic search
  • Hugging Face — LLM course

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Encode ten short public or synthetic financial headlines and calculate cosine similarities.
  2. Retrieve top three closest items for two research queries and inspect ranking errors.
  3. Store embedding model version, text timestamp, and source metadata alongside vectors.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Similarity is not truth, causation, or contemporaneous availability. General text embedding models may overfit to familiar names and phrases.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Produce a small searchable text collection and a written error analysis of two retrieval examples.

fields.topic_name: LLM evaluation, timestamps and point-in-time availability
fields.description:
Core lesson

Financial text creates severe point-in-time leakage risks. A filing's fiscal-period end is not its public filing timestamp; a headline may be updated after initial release, and a model may have been pretrained on events from later periods. Every document needs publication timestamp, access timestamp, version, and source. For an LLM-based labeling task, define a small rubric and evaluate outputs against manually checked labels. Measure agreement, invalid JSON rate, sensitivity to phrasing, and runtime or API cost. An impressive generated explanation is not the same as a timestamp-correct, validated signal.

Worked market example

A company's 10-Q covering the quarter ending March 31 may be filed in May. Using its reported figures for a trading decision in early April is look-ahead leakage.

What to read

  • SEC EDGAR — submissions and companyfacts APIs
  • SEC — search public EDGAR filings
  • Scikit-learn — classification and probability metrics

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Inspect SEC filing metadata and distinguish report period, filing date, and available-as-of timestamp.
  2. Write a small rubric for classifying filing headlines as positive, negative, or neutral.
  3. Evaluate 20 synthetic or public excerpts with confusion matrix and error categories.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Do not feed unpublished or employer-confidential information to a third-party model. Respect source licensing, request limits, and document revisions.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Deliver a timestamp schema, labeling rubric, and a small evaluation report with false positives/negatives.

fields.topic_name: Combining text signals with numeric market features
fields.description:
Core lesson

Numeric market features and text features live on different clocks. To combine them, join each market observation only with a document that was publicly available before the model decision cutoff. Start with interpretable low-dimensional text indicators: event category, signed sentiment proxy, or a compressed embedding, rather than concatenating huge vectors to a tiny dataset. Compare a numeric-only model against numeric-plus-text using the same chronological folds and cost assumptions. Any observed improvement must survive date-based evaluation and reasonable controls for announcement timing.

Worked market example

If an earnings headline is first available at 16:05, its features must not be joined to the same company's 15:59 market observations. A naïve date-based join would leak it.

What to read

  • Scikit-learn — ColumnTransformer for mixed data
  • SEC EDGAR — submissions and companyfacts APIs
  • Scikit-learn — common pitfalls and leakage

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Implement an as-of join using timestamped market observations and a tiny filings event table.
  2. Build numeric-only and numeric-plus-text feature matrices for the same labeled events.
  3. Test that advancing a document publication time removes it from earlier forecasts.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Text signals are sparse and market reactions occur quickly; generalization from a handful of news events is very limited.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Submit a point-in-time join with explicit tests and an ablation table showing whether text adds value.

fields.topic_name: Prototype a public-news or filing-based signal experiment
fields.description:
Core lesson

Prototype a small event study from public SEC filings rather than an unconstrained scraping project. Choose one filing type, collect a few document records with accession IDs and filing timestamps, and create a reproducible feature based on public filing text or metadata. Align events with a permitted daily price series and investigate price behavior after—not before—the publication window. If intraday timing or market price data is unavailable, frame the result as an educational event study rather than a real-time strategy. Define a control period to account for broad market moves.

Worked market example

A filing released at 18:20 ET should be compared with later eligible market returns; using that day’s close-to-close return may include movement that happened before the filing.

What to read

  • SEC EDGAR — submissions and companyfacts APIs
  • SEC — search public EDGAR filings
  • Pandas — descriptive statistics

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Query or download a small public EDGAR filings sample with documented access policy.
  2. Record accepted-time and event identifiers, and build a simple text/event feature.
  3. Create an event-time table of later available returns with missingness and selection notes.

Common mistakes and interpretation

SEC APIs have access rules and JSON schemas that change; use official documentation and do not scrape at high rates. Keep the sample modest.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Deliver a notebook with a few traceable filing events, timestamp-aware joins, and a limitations section.

fields.topic_name: Test whether text features add incremental out-of-sample value
fields.description:
Core lesson

Incremental value is the improvement contributed by text after accounting for the numeric features already known. Evaluate three models: numeric baseline, text-only, and combined features, using identical dates, labels, and thresholds. Use a frozen embedding or classification method to limit the number of tuned components. Report both the metric difference and its uncertainty across event dates. If your sample is too small for trustworthy trading conclusions, present the pipeline and falsifiable research hypothesis rather than inventing a positive result.

Worked market example

Numeric features alone may produce log loss 0.691; adding text might yield 0.690 on ten event days. That tiny change is not convincing without wider, independent testing.

What to read

  • Scikit-learn — ColumnTransformer for mixed data
  • Scikit-learn — probability calibration and reliability diagrams
  • SEC EDGAR — submissions and companyfacts APIs

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Train the three model variants under a shared chronological protocol.
  2. Ablate the text features and compute differences in log loss and Brier score.
  3. Inspect two cases where text helped and two where it hurt, and identify possible confounders.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Do not treat random textual document splits as out-of-sample trading evaluation; events in a company or period may be closely related.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Finish Week 11 with a small multimodal research note including negative or inconclusive findings honestly.

fields.topic_name: Research reports and experiment reproducibility
fields.description:
Core lesson

A research report is an argument supported by reproducible evidence, not a dashboard of attractive figures. State a falsifiable question, describe data provenance and limitations, define features and targets mathematically, record chronological evaluation design, and compare models against baselines. Report metrics with uncertainty and cost assumptions. An experiment manifest should include code commit, data hash or accessible source, random seed, dependency versions, split IDs, and exact run command. A reader should be able to distinguish what was known before training from what was selected afterward.

Worked market example

A claim such as “LSTM is better” is incomplete. A reproducible claim is: “On the frozen last-three-session test, the LSTM reduced mean log loss by 0.002 relative to logistic regression; day-block CI includes zero.”

What to read

  • MLflow — experiment tracking
  • GitHub — repository README documentation
  • Introduction to Statistical Learning — free textbook

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Draft a report outline with question, hypotheses, data, methods, results, and limitations.
  2. Record command-line parameters, dependency lockfile, and dataset lineage for one experiment.
  3. Reproduce a summary table from a clean environment or second checkout.

Common mistakes and interpretation

A single published notebook is not necessarily reproducible if it silently requires proprietary data, an absolute path, or undocumented preprocessing.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Produce a research-paper-style methods section and evidence that another run reproduces key results.

fields.topic_name: Quant probability and statistics interview topics
fields.description:
Core lesson

Quant interviews commonly test conditional probability, expectation, independence, confidence intervals, linear regression, probability calibration, and time-series validation. They also evaluate whether you can reason from first principles under uncertainty. Practice separating a statistical model's assumptions from the numerical answer. For coding questions, write correct Python with time-complexity reasoning, but allocate more interview time to the mathematical intuition you are developing. Use market examples only when they genuinely illuminate the probability problem.

Worked market example

A test has 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity for a condition that occurs 1% of the time. The probability of the condition after a positive test is much lower than 95%; calculate it using Bayes’ theorem.

What to read

  • OpenIntro Statistics — free textbook
  • Introduction to Statistical Learning — free textbook
  • Google — machine learning crash course

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Solve three Bayes/conditional-probability questions without code, then verify with Python.
  2. Derive ordinary least-squares loss and explain regularization qualitatively.
  3. Describe how you would validate an imbalance predictor on serially correlated data.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Memorized formulas without explaining the sample space or assumptions will fail harder research discussions.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Prepare three written explanations and practice presenting each aloud in under four minutes.

fields.topic_name: Explaining model limitations and business relevance
fields.description:
Core lesson

A credible researcher explains what the model cannot establish. Forecast performance is conditioned on a dataset, horizon, regime, selection process, and implementation. Discuss drift, survivorship bias, limited instrument coverage, unreliable fill simulation, and uncertainty around costs. Translate engineering tradeoffs into business relevance: a small AUC improvement may be worth less than lower latency or more robust behavior. State risk of loss and monitoring requirements without implying profits. Your production market-data experience is valuable because it helps identify silent data issues before they become false research discoveries.

Worked market example

A model that improves log loss but takes 30 ms longer to infer may be unusable for a strategy whose opportunity window is only a few milliseconds.

What to read

  • Scikit-learn — common pitfalls and leakage
  • QuantStats — performance metrics and reports
  • MLflow — experiment tracking

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Write a limitations section distinguishing statistical, data, and execution risks.
  2. Create a decision memo comparing a simple model against the strongest ML model on performance and latency.
  3. Prepare an explanation of when you would stop a strategy or revert to a baseline in production.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Do not claim causality or realistic capacity from a public one-day sample. Make uncertainty explicit and quantified where possible.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Deliver a two-minute spoken summary and a written model-risk checklist grounded in your actual experiments.

fields.topic_name: Prepare polished GitHub repository and research report
fields.description:
Core lesson

A professional portfolio needs a discoverable narrative and runnable implementation. Organize your repository around data ingest, schema validation, features, split generation, model training, evaluation, simulator, tests, and reports. Include an environment setup, sample dataset instructions, legal/licensing limitations, and exact commands to regenerate plots. Keep configuration separate from code and avoid absolute paths. Explain the research question and negative results prominently in README, rather than burying them in notebook outputs. Use small public or synthetic fixtures for unit tests.

Worked market example

A hiring manager should be able to open README, run one short command on a synthetic sample, and see a baseline evaluation with a clear statement that it is a demonstration, not a proven alpha.

What to read

  • GitHub — repository README documentation
  • MLflow — experiment tracking
  • LOBSTER — free order-book sample files

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Create a clean repository tree and document dataset acquisition without redistributing restricted files.
  2. Add a one-command small reproducible experiment and run it in a fresh virtual environment.
  3. Publish a concise report with model comparisons, confidence intervals, and backtest assumptions.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Never commit company code, data, secrets, credentials, or proprietary modeling details. Review Git history before publishing.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Finish with a public or safely shareable portfolio repository and an independently reproducible example.

fields.topic_name: Practice research defense and apply to suitable roles
fields.description:
Core lesson

A research defense tests whether you truly understand experimental choices. Practice answering why you selected the label horizon, which split prevents leakage, whether imbalance adds value beyond price momentum, how much uncertainty remains, and which cost assumptions invalidate trading profitability. Connect your background in FIX, market-data normalization, HDF5 backtesting, and distributed Python to the new research stack without claiming professional alpha research you have not done. Target quant research engineering and applied ML research roles initially, then deeper researcher roles as evidence grows.

Worked market example

An interviewer asks why random-split AUC exceeded walk-forward AUC. A strong answer identifies dependence and possible leakage, describes controlled tests, and acknowledges genuine distribution shift as another explanation.

What to read

  • Introduction to Statistical Learning — free textbook
  • Scikit-learn — common pitfalls and leakage
  • GitHub — repository README documentation

Your 60-minute study session

15 minutes: read the linked source and take notes on definitions and assumptions; 10 minutes: reproduce the worked example by hand or in Python; 30 minutes: complete the scoped implementation tasks; 5 minutes: record your evidence, limitations, and follow-up questions.

Hands-on exercises

  1. Deliver a five-minute project defense including question, data, methods, result, and failures.
  2. Answer ten technical follow-ups about probability, validation, microstructure, costs, and reproducibility.
  3. Draft tailored resume bullets and identify target role requirements that your portfolio does and does not yet demonstrate.

Common mistakes and interpretation

Do not claim guaranteed performance or senior quant research experience merely because the software is production-quality.

Checkpoint before completion

Evidence to save: Complete Week 12 with a final research deck, interview answer bank, and a prioritized application list.
